lessons.title: Reading 4-3-3
lessons.objective: You can read a formation from its numbers.

payload.prompt: What do the numbers in 4-3-3 mean?

options.text: Four strikers, three midfielders, three defenders
Four defenders, three midfielders, three forwards
Four wins, three draws, three losses

explanation.correct: Exactly. Formations list defenders first, then midfielders, then forwards.
explanation.incorrect: Formation numbers count outfield players from defence to attack: defenders, midfielders, forwards.
explanation.sayThisLine: Four back, three in midfield, front three.

payload.prompt: Match formation terms to their meanings.

pairs.definition: Two centre-backs and two full-backs, the most common defensive shape.
Four defenders, three central midfielders and three forwards: striker and two wingers.
In 4-3-3, usually a striker and wingers hugging the touchlines to stretch teams.

explanation.summary: 4-3-3 balances defence, control and attacking width. The back four is its defensive base.
explanation.sayThisLine: Back four, three eights, and the strikers out wide.

payload.prompt: In 4-3-3, the wingers play wide. True or false?

scene.alt: A 4-3-3 formation with two wingers wide on the touchlines, a striker in the middle, three central midfielders and a back four.

explanation.correct: True. In a 4-3-3 the wingers play wide, close to the touchlines, to stretch the defence and create room for the striker and midfield.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, a 4-3-3 uses wingers wide to stretch teams horizontally and create crossing chances.
explanation.sayThisLine: Wingers on the touchline, striker in the middle.

payload.prompt: Complete the 4-3-3 structure.
payload.template: A 4-3-3 has {{defenders}} defenders, {{midfielders}} midfielders and {{forwards}} forwards.

explanation.correct: Right. Four-three-three: a back four, three central midfielders and two wingers with a striker.
explanation.incorrect: 4-3-3 means four outfield defenders, three midfielders and three attacking players total.

statement.speaker: Kai
statement.text: Our 4-3-3 stretches teams with the wingers hugging the touchlines.

payload.question: What's the goal of this shape?

options.text: To make the pitch wider and harder to defend
To make the team harder to attack
To pull defenders wide and create space
To have more midfielders than defenders

payload.translation: By keeping wingers wide, teams open the pitch horizontally, forcing full-backs to stretch, which creates gaps.

followUps.line: Does the left winger have a good cross?
followUps.why: Tests knowledge of your team's style.

followUps.line: Do the full-backs get tired covering that much ground?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask if the wingers score or create.

payload.prompt: Which positions make up a back four?

options.text: Four centre-backs
Two centre-backs and two full-backs
Goalkeeper and three defenders

explanation.correct: Right. A back four has two centre-backs in the middle and one full-back on each side.
explanation.incorrect: The back four is two centre-backs plus left and right full-backs, not including the keeper.
explanation.sayThisLine: Back four: centre-backs in the middle, full-backs on the wings.

payload.prompt: Tap the front three in this 4-3-3.

diagram.alt: Overhead diagram of a 4-3-3: goalkeeper at the bottom, a back four, a deep midfielder with two central midfielders ahead, and a front three.

explanation.correct: Right. The front three is the striker in the middle and a winger on each side.
explanation.incorrect: In a 4-3-3 the front three are the striker and the two wingers. The deeper players are midfielders.
explanation.sayThisLine: Front three: the striker in the middle and a winger on each side.

lessons.title: 4-2-3-1 and 4-4-2
lessons.objective: You can explain the difference between 4-2-3-1 and 4-4-2.

payload.prompt: Match each formation to its shape.

pairs.definition: Four defenders, two holding midfielders, three attacking players behind one striker. Built for control and transition.
Two banks of four: defenders and midfielders form a flat line, two strikers up front. Compact and simple.
A midfielder who sits deep to break up play and screen the defence in the 4-2-3-1.

explanation.summary: 4-2-3-1 adds a 10 behind the 9 for creativity; 4-4-2 keeps it flat with two 9s.
explanation.sayThisLine: 4-2-3-1 has a creator, 4-4-2 has two strikers.

payload.prompt: How does 4-2-3-1 differ from 4-4-2?

options.text: 4-2-3-1 has a number 10 behind the striker; 4-4-2 doesn't
4-4-2 has more midfielders
4-2-3-1 has two strikers; 4-4-2 has one

explanation.correct: Exactly. In 4-2-3-1, the 10 (attacking midfielder) sits behind the lone 9. In 4-4-2, you have two strikers.
explanation.incorrect: 4-2-3-1 uses one striker with a 10 to create for him. 4-4-2 uses two strikers and no attacking midfielder.
explanation.sayThisLine: 4-2-3-1 puts the 10 behind the 9.

payload.prompt: In 4-2-3-1, the two deep midfielders screen the defence. True or false?

scene.alt: A 4-2-3-1 with two midfielders sitting deep between the back four and the attacking three.

explanation.correct: True. The two 6s sit between the line and the 10 to protect the defence and win the ball back.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, the two holding midfielders (often called sixes) are the shield in front of the back four.
explanation.sayThisLine: The double six sits deep to protect the back line.

payload.prompt: 4-4-2 has two compact banks of four, but the midfield can get outnumbered. True or false?

scene.alt: A 4-4-2 with defenders and midfielders in two flat lines and two strikers up front, facing a three-man midfield.

explanation.correct: True. The two banks of four are compact and simple, but only two central midfielders can be outnumbered by a three-man midfield.
explanation.incorrect: 4-4-2 is compact and simple, but with only two central midfielders it can be outnumbered in the middle by a team playing three there.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two banks of four, but they were overrun in midfield.

payload.prompt: Compare the number of strikers in each formation.
payload.template: 4-2-3-1 has {{one}} striker with a 10 behind him, while 4-4-2 has {{two}} strikers.

explanation.correct: Right. One striker and a 10 in 4-2-3-1 gives creativity; two strikers in 4-4-2 keeps it direct.
explanation.incorrect: 4-2-3-1 has one 9 and a creator behind him. 4-4-2 has two 9s attacking together.

statement.speaker: Alex
statement.text: In a 4-2-3-1 the ten sits behind the nine.

payload.question: Why would a team choose this?

options.text: To have a playmaker create chances for one striker
To have more attacking power
To balance control and creativity
Because it's easier to defend

payload.translation: The 10 (attacking midfielder) unlocks the defence for one striker, giving control and creativity from the centre.

followUps.line: Is your 10 more creative or more physical?
Does the 10 score or just create?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, say you're still learning the midfield roles.

lessons.title: Back threes and wing-backs
lessons.objective: You can explain why some teams play with three centre-backs.

payload.prompt: How many centre-backs do teams have in a back three?

options.text: One
Two
Three

explanation.correct: Right. Three centre-backs give cover and let full-backs become wing-backs.
explanation.incorrect: A back three uses three central defenders, usually all centre-backs, plus wing-backs on the flanks.
explanation.sayThisLine: Three centre-backs, that's the back three.

payload.prompt: Match the terms in a back-three shape.

pairs.definition: Three centre-backs across the defensive line, giving extra cover in the middle
A wide player who defends the flank and pushes forward to attack it
What a back three often becomes without the ball when the wing-backs drop in

explanation.summary: A back three trades a spare midfielder for an extra centre-back, and the wing-backs stretch the pitch. Without the ball it often becomes a back five.
explanation.sayThisLine: The wing-backs do double the running in a back three.

payload.prompt: In a back three, wing-backs must defend and attack. True or false?

scene.alt: A back-three system with a wing-back running the full length of the flank, defending and overlapping.

explanation.correct: True. Wing-backs cover the whole flank; they're defenders who push forward to attack.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, wing-backs defend their flank and then burst forward to cross or overlap the winger.
explanation.sayThisLine: Wing-backs are defenders who attack; they run the whole game.

payload.prompt: Complete the back-three system.
payload.template: A back three has {{cbs}} centre-backs and {{wbs}} wing-backs, and often drops into a back {{line}} when defending.

explanation.correct: Right. Three centre-backs plus a wing-back on each side makes a back five once the wing-backs drop in to defend.
explanation.incorrect: A back three is three centre-backs with a wing-back on each flank. When the wing-backs drop in to defend, the line becomes a back five.

statement.speaker: Morgan
statement.text: In a back five the wing-backs do double the running.

payload.question: Why do wing-backs run so much?

options.text: They defend their flank and attack down it
They have to cover for the midfielders
The team is trying to tire opponents
They must cover the whole line up and down

payload.translation: Wing-backs defend their flank and then run forward to overlap and cross, covering more ground than traditional full-backs.

followUps.line: Is your wing-back more physical or technical?
When does the wing-back attack vs defend?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You can admit wing-back is demanding.

payload.prompt: What is one reason a team might play a back three?

options.text: An extra centre-back for cover, with wing-backs providing width
It needs no midfielders at all
It guarantees a clean sheet

explanation.correct: Right. A back three adds central cover, and the wing-backs give the team width. The trade-off is that the wings need players with a lot of stamina.
explanation.incorrect: A back three is about cover in the middle plus width from wing-backs. It is not a guarantee of anything, and teams still need midfielders.

lessons.title: Name that shape (sim)
lessons.objective: You can read a team's shape from its movement.

payload.prompt: Why do commentators say it's not the numbers, it's the movement?

options.text: Because players move between lines and change shape in a match
Because formations are never written down
Because shirts have numbers that change

explanation.correct: Right. Formation numbers are a starting picture. Players rotate and shift, so what matters is how the shape moves with and without the ball.
explanation.incorrect: The numbers on a team sheet are only a starting picture. Players move between the lines during play, so the shape you see can change from moment to moment.
explanation.sayThisLine: It says 4-3-3 on paper but it looks like a 3-2-5 with the ball.

payload.prompt: Match the possession state to the shape change.

pairs.definition: The team stays compact, with lines close together, to block space, for example in a 4-4-2 or 4-5-1
The team spreads out to find space and create chances
A team changes shape when it wins or loses the ball

explanation.summary: Shape isn't fixed; it changes with possession. Defending is compact; attacking is spread.
explanation.sayThisLine: They look like a 4-3-3 but they defend in a 4-5-1.

payload.prompt: Complete the compactness definition.
payload.template: A team that is {{shape}} keeps the gaps between its lines {{gaps}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Compact defence means no room to play into. Spread means width and depth to attack.
explanation.incorrect: Compactness means small gaps between players and lines. Attackers hate small gaps.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: They look like a 4-3-3 but they defend in a 4-5-1.

payload.question: What do they mean?

options.text: The shape changes with and without the ball
The team plays two different formations each match
They're compact when defending
The formation is unstable

payload.translation: In possession they spread to 4-3-3; without it they compact to 4-5-1 to stop attacks.

followUps.line: Do they defend high or drop back?
Does the shape change quickly after turnovers?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Most top teams shift shape constantly; it's expected.

payload.prompt: Formation numbers like 4-3-3 describe exact player positions. True or false?

scene.alt: A formation showing rough layers rather than exact spots.

explanation.correct: False. Formations are rough layers, not exact spots. Players move within the layer.
explanation.incorrect: Formations describe layers (back, mid, front), not where every player stands exactly.
explanation.sayThisLine: Numbers are guidelines, not fixed spots.

lessons.title: With the ball, without it
lessons.objective: You can explain how shape changes in and out of possession.

payload.prompt: When a team has the ball, how does the shape change?

options.text: It gets more compact to protect possession
It spreads out to find space and create chances
It stays exactly the same

explanation.correct: Right. Teams spread with the ball to stretch the defence and find gaps to exploit.
explanation.incorrect: When attacking, teams spread out wide and deep to pull the defence apart.
explanation.sayThisLine: The ball means we spread and look for space.

payload.prompt: When a team loses the ball, how does the shape change?

options.text: It gets more compact to block space
It spreads out to press higher
It stays spread to keep attacking

explanation.correct: Exactly. Teams compact after losing the ball to reduce space and stop the counter.
explanation.incorrect: Without the ball, teams compact their lines to stop attackers finding space.
explanation.sayThisLine: Lose the ball and we're tight, no gaps.

payload.prompt: Complete the shape change rule.
payload.template: With the ball, a team {{with}} to attack; without it, the team {{without}} to defend.

explanation.correct: Right. Spread to attack (width and depth), compact to defend (no gaps).
explanation.incorrect: Teams spread when attacking to stretch defenders and compact when defending to block space.

payload.prompt: Match the possession state to the shape goal.

pairs.definition: Spread shape to find gaps, isolate defenders, and create attacks in space.
Compact shape to block passing lanes, reduce space and stop counter-attacks.
When possession changes, shape shifts immediately; speed matters.

explanation.summary: Good teams shift shape instantly as possession changes. It's a rhythm, not a freeze.
explanation.sayThisLine: The best teams flip shape as soon as it changes hands.

statement.speaker: Riley
statement.text: They stayed compact, there were no gaps to play into.

payload.question: What's this saying about their defence?

options.text: They were well-organized without the ball
The defence made no mistakes
They gave the ball away easily
No space existed between their lines

payload.translation: The defending team kept tight lines and gaps small, making it hard for attackers to find a passing lane.

followUps.line: Did they press high or sit back?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, say organisation is key to good defence.

payload.prompt: A team's shape should change when possession changes. True or false?

scene.alt: A team's shape shifting from spread (attacking) to compact (defending).

explanation.correct: True. The fastest teams shift shape instantly; it gives them an edge.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, shape changes with possession. The transition speed separates good teams from great ones.
explanation.sayThisLine: Best teams flip shape the moment it changes hands.

lessons.title: Compact lines and space
lessons.objective: You can explain compactness, width and depth.

payload.prompt: What makes a defence compact?

options.text: All players are on the same line
Small gaps between lines and players
No defensive midfielders on the pitch

explanation.correct: Right. Compactness means tight spacing vertically and horizontally, no room to play into.
explanation.incorrect: A compact defence has small gaps between its defenders and lines; attackers find nowhere to receive.
explanation.sayThisLine: Compact defence: nothing between the lines.

payload.prompt: Match the attacking principle to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Stretching the pitch horizontally by placing players on the flanks to pull defenders wide.
Stretching the pitch vertically (forward and backward) to separate the defence into layers.
Pull defenders both wide and deep to isolate them, then attack the gaps.

explanation.summary: Width without depth is predictable; depth without width is narrow. Great attacks use both.
explanation.sayThisLine: Width on the wing, depth from the striker.

payload.prompt: Complete the space principle.
payload.template: Attackers create space with {{width}} (across the pitch) and {{depth}} (up and down it), pulling the defence {{dir}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Width and depth pull defenders in different directions, opening gaps to exploit.
explanation.incorrect: Width spreads defenders horizontally, depth spreads them vertically. Together they create space.

payload.prompt: In a compact defence, gaps between lines are small. True or false?

scene.alt: A compact defensive shape with tight spacing between lines.

explanation.correct: True. Compact defence removes space between lines, making it hard to play through.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, compactness means small gaps vertically between defenders and horizontal rows.
explanation.sayThisLine: Compact means no space to play into.

statement.speaker: Jordan
statement.text: Width on the wing, depth from the striker, that's how you open a defence.

payload.question: Why does this strategy work?

options.text: Defenders can't cover all that ground at once
It's direct play
It pulls defenders in different directions
The keeper can't react in time

payload.translation: A winger stretches the defence horizontally, a striker pushes depth, and when defenders are spread, they leave gaps to exploit.

followUps.line: Does your winger create space or your striker?
What's the main threat: crosses or through balls?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Width and depth basics; fine to ask how your team creates space.

payload.prompt: Why do teams play wingers on the touchline?

options.text: To create width and pull full-backs wide
To avoid the midfield
To make the pitch feel bigger

explanation.correct: Exactly. Wingers on the line stretch the pitch horizontally and overload the flanks.
explanation.incorrect: Wingers wide create horizontal stretch (width), pulling defenders out and leaving space in the middle.
explanation.sayThisLine: Wingers stretched them sideways; we had acres in the middle.

lessons.title: Half-spaces and between the lines (sim)
lessons.objective: You can find the half-space and the pocket between lines.

payload.prompt: Match these key attacking zones.

pairs.definition: Vertical channels between the wide and central areas; favourite spots for creative players.
Horizontal space between a defence's back line and midfield line; dangerous for a turning attacker.
Paths between teammates that are open; angles and movement create them.

explanation.summary: Half-spaces and between-the-lines are where attackers live. Defending them is key.
explanation.sayThisLine: He got between the lines and turned into space.

payload.prompt: Tap the two half-spaces in the attacking third.

diagram.alt: The attacking third split into five vertical channels: two wide, two half-spaces beside the centre, and one central.

explanation.correct: Right. The half-spaces are the channels between the wide areas and the centre. Creators love them because defenders have to choose who picks the ball up.
explanation.incorrect: The half-space sits between the wing and the centre, one on each side. The wing channel and the central channel are the other zones.
explanation.sayThisLine: He lives in the half-space, between the full-back and the centre-back.

payload.prompt: Complete the 'between the lines' definition.
payload.template: Between the lines is the space {{where}} a defence's back line and its midfield line, where a {{who}} attacker is {{risk}}.

explanation.correct: Right. When an attacker turns in the space between lines, they have sight of goal and the whole pitch.
explanation.incorrect: Between-the-lines is the horizontal gap where a player turning with the ball is most dangerous.

statement.speaker: Alex
statement.text: He got the ball between the lines and turned.

payload.question: Why is that so dangerous?

options.text: He can see the whole pitch from there
He's facing forward, not sideways
The defence is already committed
The keeper is out of position

payload.translation: Between the lines, an attacker faces forward with a view of goal and space around him. The defence is stretched.

followUps.line: Who on your team finds that space best?
Does the 10 or the 8 spend more time there?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Between the lines is a key attacking idea; it's good to learn.

payload.prompt: How does a team open up a passing lane?

options.text: Teammates move to angles the defenders cannot cover
Everyone stands in a straight line
They only pass backwards

explanation.correct: Right. Passing lanes do not appear by magic. Runs and angled positions pull defenders away and leave a clear path for the ball.
explanation.incorrect: A lane opens when players position themselves at angles the defenders cannot cover. Standing in a line or passing backwards leaves the lane blocked.
explanation.sayThisLine: His run opened up the passing lane.

lessons.title: Triangles and switches
lessons.objective: You can explain triangles, overloads and a switch of play.

payload.prompt: Match the tactical shape to its purpose.

pairs.definition: Three players in a triangle give the ball carrier two close passing options
More players than opponents in one zone creates a free man and forces defenders out of position.
A quick long pass from one flank to the other to attack the weak side before the defence resets.

explanation.summary: Triangles ensure safe possession; overloads create a free man; switches attack fresh areas.
explanation.sayThisLine: Triangles everywhere, an overload on the left, and the switch opened the right.

payload.prompt: Why do coaches like triangles between players?

options.text: They look nice on a coaching board
The ball carrier gets two close passing options
They stop the opponent from tackling

explanation.correct: Exactly. A triangle gives the player on the ball two short options, which makes it easy to keep possession and move play forward.
explanation.incorrect: Triangles give the ball carrier two nearby passing options. That helps a team keep the ball and find a way forward.
explanation.sayThisLine: Triangles everywhere, always an easy pass.

payload.prompt: What's the goal of an overload in a zone?

options.text: To tire the defenders quickly
To create a free man with numbers
To make the field more crowded

explanation.correct: Right. If you have more players than the opponent in one zone, someone is free.
explanation.incorrect: An overload puts more attackers than defenders in a zone so one attacker is unmarked.
explanation.sayThisLine: We overloaded the left and the winger was free.

payload.prompt: Complete the switch-of-play description.
payload.template: A switch of play is a {{speed}}, {{length}} pass from one flank to the other, played {{when}} the defence can reset.

explanation.correct: Right. A switch happens fast, while the defence is still committed to the other side.
explanation.incorrect: A switch is a quick long pass to the opposite flank, attacking before defenders reposition.

statement.speaker: Casey
statement.text: The switch was perfect, the winger had acres of space.

payload.question: Why did the switch create space?

options.text: The defence was still on the other side
The winger ran faster
The opponents weren't alert
The weak-side defender was outnumbered

payload.translation: The ball was switched quickly before the defence could reset to the new flank, leaving the winger space to attack.

followUps.line: Who delivered the switch on your team?
Does the switch come from the back or midfield?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, say switches are fast passes to the weak side.

payload.prompt: Three attackers against two defenders in one zone is an overload. True or false?

scene.alt: Three attackers face two defenders in one zone of the pitch, leaving one attacker free.

explanation.correct: True. Three against two means one is free. That's the overload.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, if you have more players than the opponent in a zone, an attacker has space to work.
explanation.sayThisLine: Three against two is an overload; someone's free.
